chunks: Muhammad ibn Hammam narrated: Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Malik narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Madani narrated to us: Ali ibn Asbat narrated from Muhammad ibn Sinan from Dawud ibn Kathir al-Raqqi who said: I said to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him): 'May I be your ransom, this matter has been long upon us until our hearts became constricted and we died of sadness.' He said: 'This matter will be most despaired of and most distressing when a caller will call from the Heaven with the name of the Qa'im and the name of his father.' I said to him: 'May I be your ransom, what is his name?' He said: 'His name is the name of a Prophet, and the name of his father is the name of a Guardian (Wasi).'

key_terms.الْقَائِمِ: The Raiser/Imam who will rise to establish justice
key_terms.الْوَصِيّ: The Successor/Guardian, often referring to an Imam or specific successor
key_terms.جَعَلْتُ فَدَاكَ: May I be your ransom (a phrase of deep respect and devotion)

ai.seo_question: What is the name of the Qa'im and his father according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) addresses the psychological toll of the prolonged occultation, noting that despair peaks just before the heralding call of the Qa'im from heaven. This tradition highlights the theological concept of 'Istishhad' (waiting for relief) and confirms the Imam's identity by linking his name to a Prophet and his father's to a Wasi, reinforcing the continuity of divine authority. The narration serves as a comfort to the Shia community, framing their sorrow as a precursor to the ultimate manifestation of justice.
